claims.text: The alloy studied is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The additively manufactured alloy contains dual nanoprecipitates.
High-temperature oxidation will cause significant atomic-scale elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate–oxide interfaces.
Al and Ti are oxidation-resistant elements in this alloy.
Al and Ti will preferentially segregate to nanoprecipitate–oxide interfaces during oxidation.
Interfacial segregation of Al and Ti will promote protective oxide formation.
The nanoprecipitates have a fairly homogeneous composition before oxidation.
Oxidation in air at approximately 800–1000°C induces elemental diffusion and oxidation in the alloy.
Nanoprecipitates act as localized reservoirs of oxidation-resistant elements.
The nanoprecipitates influence the formation and composition of the oxide scale.
High-temperature exposure drives diffusion of key elements from nanoprecipitates toward the oxide front.
APT provides three-dimensional atomic-scale compositional mapping capable of detecting Al and Ti accumulation at interfaces.
APT will reveal pronounced Al and Ti segregation at nanoprecipitate–oxide interfaces in oxidized samples relative to the unoxidized baseline.
Al and Ti segregation will correlate with improved local oxidation resistance.
Before oxidation, the nanoprecipitates are uniformly distributed and lack significant elemental segregation.
The extent and kinetics of elemental redistribution may vary with nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and small compositional variations.
